title: Sharps, blood and clinical waste escalation
audience: Cleaners and cleaning supervisors who work in medical and dental clinics in Australia. The lesson teaches recognition and escalation of sharps, blood and clinical waste, not handling of them.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NHMRC, Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019) (no page date shown; document dated 2019); NDIS Practice Standards and Quality Indicators, Version 4, Core Module (cover date November 2021; no page date shown).
learningOutcomes: Recognise a sharp, a blood or body-fluid contamination and a clinical waste container, and explain why a cleaner does not handle them.
State the escalation steps for each, including keeping others away and calling the designated clinical contact.
Describe the exposure response if a cleaner is stuck, cut or splashed.
Record the item, location, time and person notified, without handling the item.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson: recognition and escalation only
instruction.body: This lesson teaches you to recognise sharps, blood and body-fluid contamination, and clinical waste, and to escalate them. It does not teach you to handle, collect, sort, compact, transport or dispose of them. Those tasks are performed by staff the clinic has trained and authorised for them, under the clinic's waste procedure and any state or territory requirement. Reprocessing, disinfection for reusable devices and sterilisation are outside this course, and are authorised only by the manufacturer's instructions and the clinic procedure.

instruction.heading: Recognising sharps
instruction.body: A sharp is any object that can puncture or cut the skin, such as a needle, a lancet, a scalpel blade, a broken glass ampoule or a dental instrument tip. A sharp that may be contaminated must be treated as a hazard even if it looks clean. Common places to find them include the floor beside a chair, in a drawer, between cushions, in a bin that has not been sorted, and in a corridor after a procedure. Do not reach into a bin, drawer or cushion without looking first. If you cannot see the whole of an area, do not reach into the gap. Ask for the area to be checked by the trained person.

instruction.heading: Blood and body-fluid contamination
instruction.body: Blood and body fluids are treated as potentially infectious. A visible spot of blood on a chair, a bench or the floor, or a dressing with a stain, is a contamination that you do not clean unless you have been trained and authorised for that specific task. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare recommend that anyone cleaning a spill wears gloves and other personal protective equipment appropriate to the task, and the clinic's procedure defines which spills a cleaner may attend. For anything beyond the clinic's authorised list, restrict access, keep people away, and call the designated clinical or spill contact. Do not wipe the spot to make it less visible.

instruction.heading: Clinical waste containers
instruction.body: Clinical waste containers, including sharps containers and bags for clinical waste, are labelled and placed by the clinic. Do not open, move, tip, compact or reposition a sharps container, and do not push items into it. If a container is full, damaged, overfilled or not closed, leave it as found, keep people away from it, and tell the designated clinical contact. Do not carry clinical waste from one area to another on your trolley. The NHMRC guidelines state that facilities must follow state and territory clinical waste laws.

instruction.heading: Exposure and the stop-and-report response
instruction.body: If you are stuck by a sharp, cut, or splashed by blood or another body fluid on broken skin or the eyes, nose or mouth, stop the task immediately. Remove yourself from the immediate area, and follow the clinic's exposure procedure at once. Do not squeeze the wound to make it bleed. Tell the designated clinical contact and your supervisor the same shift, and record the exposure with the time, the source where known, the first aid given and the person notified. The clinic decides any follow-up assessment, and the cleaner does not decide it alone.

procedure: Before reaching into any bin, drawer, cushion or gap, look for sharps and contamination, and keep your hands out of spaces you cannot see into.
If you see a sharp, stop, keep others away, and call the designated sharps response person under the clinic procedure.
If you see blood or body fluid beyond your authorised list, restrict access, keep people away, and call the designated clinical or spill contact.
Do not open, move, tip, compact or push items into any sharps container or clinical waste container. Leave it as found and report it if it is full, damaged or open.
If you are stuck, cut or splashed, stop, remove yourself from the area, follow the exposure procedure, and report the same shift.
Record the item or contamination, its location, the time, the person called and the outcome, without having handled the item.

workedExamples.situation: While cleaning a dental operatory, you see a small capped needle lying beside the chair leg, partly under the chair base.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not pick it up or move it with your hands. Keep others away from the area, and call the designated sharps response person under the clinic procedure. Record the location, the time and the person called. Do not continue cleaning the area around the needle until the trained person has dealt with it.

workedExamples.situation: A clinical waste container in a corridor is overfilled and its lid will not close. A colleague asks you to push the lid down and carry the container to the store on your trolley.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Do not push the lid, tip or move the container, and do not carry clinical waste on your trolley. Keep people away, leave the container as found, tell the designated clinical contact, and record the report and the time. The clinic's trained staff move it under its procedure.

commonErrors.error: Reaching into a bin, drawer or cushion without looking, and being stuck by a sharp.
commonErrors.prevention: Look first. Keep hands out of spaces you cannot see into, and ask for the area to be checked.

commonErrors.error: Picking up a capped needle to move it out of the way.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not handle sharps by hand. Keep others away and call the sharps response person.

commonErrors.error: Wiping a blood spot to make the area look clean before the clinical contact arrives.
commonErrors.prevention: Restrict access and call the designated contact. Clean only the spills your clinic authorises.

commonErrors.error: Carrying an overfilled clinical waste container to the store on your trolley.
commonErrors.prevention: Leave it as found, keep people away, and report it to the designated clinical contact.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019) recommend that anyone cleaning a spill wears gloves and other personal protective equipment appropriate to the task (Recommendation 12). The clinic procedure defines which spills a cleaner may attend.

The NDIS Practice Standards, Version 4 of November 2021, Core Module, require policies for storing, handling and disposing of infectious waste, including used PPE, that incidents involving infectious material are reported, recorded and investigated, and that workers who handle waste are trained. Where the clinic is an NDIS provider, these apply to the clinic.

Licence notice: Collecting, transporting or disposing of clinical waste may need a state or territory permit or licence. Completing this lesson does not grant any waste handling, transport or disposal authority.

qualityStandard: The learner identifies a sharp, a blood contamination and a full clinical waste container in supplied scenarios, and states that none is handled by hand.
The learner gives the escalation steps for each supplied item in order, including keeping others away and the person to call.
The learner describes the exposure response in order and names the person to notify.
The learner records a supplied item and its escalation without having handled it.
documentationEvidence: Item or contamination type, location, time, and the person called
Any container left as found, with the report made and the time
Any exposure, with the first aid given, the source where known and the person notified
summary: Sharps, blood and clinical waste are recognised and escalated. They are not handled by a cleaner unless trained and authorised.
Look before reaching. Keep hands out of spaces you cannot see into.
Do not open, move, tip or push items into a sharps or clinical waste container. Leave it as found and report.
After an exposure, stop, follow the clinic procedure, and report the same shift.

knowledgeChecks.question: You see a capped needle lying on the floor beside a chair. What is the correct action?
options: Pick it up with a tissue and place it in the general bin.
Do not handle it. Keep others away and call the designated sharps response person.
Move it under the chair so it is out of the way until the end of the shift.

knowledgeChecks.question: A clinical waste container is overfilled and will not close. What should you do?
options: Push the lid down and carry the container to the store before the end of the shift
Tip the contents into a bag to make room in the container, so the lid can be closed
Leave it as found, keep people away, and report it to the designated clinical contact.

knowledgeChecks.question: You are cut by a sharp during a task. What is the correct first step?
options: Stop the task, remove yourself from the area, and follow the clinic exposure procedure at once.
Squeeze the wound to make it bleed, then finish the task before reporting the cut
Wrap the cut and wait until the end of the shift to report it to the clinic manager
